entries.title: Germany: Sven Schulze takes on the far-right AfD
entries.summary: The AfD is way ahead in the polls in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt. But the young state premier insists he can stop the far-right from leading a government for the first time since World War II.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany: Sven Schulze takes on the far-right AfD

August 31, 2026

The AfD is way ahead in the polls in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt. But the young state premier insists he can stop the far-right from leading a government for the first time since World War II.

"It's far from decided." State Premier Sven Schulze likes to repeat his big campaign message over and over again ahead of the impending election in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt on September 6. His audience, however, rarely responds with enthusiasm.

The German public and international media alike are watching this election closely. Never before has the Alternative for Germany (AfD) — classified by the domestic intelligence agency as "confirmed right-wing extremist" — had a better chance to take over a state government. The party is polling at over 40% compared to Schulze's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) at around 23%.

Schulze is hoping the AfD will stay below 50% and so be unable to secure a majority in the state parliament — and, with no other party willing to join it in a coalition, the AfD would be unable to form a government. That would leave it up to Schulze to form a coalition, perhaps with as many as three partners, and remain in office. "We are fighting for every single voter right now," he told DW on August 7.

Young, family man, engineer, cyclist

Schulze was just eleven years old at the time of German reunification. Now, at 47, the qualified industrial engineer and father of three is the youngest of Germany's 16 state premiers. 

He only took over leadership of the state at the end of January, when his predecessor, Reiner Haseloff — then aged 71 — retired after nearly 15 years in office. The early handover to Schulze was supposed to improve the younger man's prospects in the state election. After all, a sitting premier is said to enjoy an "incumbency bonus."

Schulze is now touring the state of two million inhabitants. On some days, he has been seen out and about on his bicycle, complete with cycling jersey and helmet, handing out ice cream on hot summer days, and engaging in small group discussions. Aware that his party leader, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, is not exactly popular in Germany right now, one of his recurring messages has been that he is not there "to sell the Berlin government's ideas to Saxony-Anhalt." Instead, he says, his task is "to bring issues from Saxony-Anhalt to Berlin." Not everyone in Merz's government is necessarily pleased about this message.

Celebrities welcome, chancellor not so much

This became particularly evident when Schulze appeared at campaign events in the state's larger cities alongside Dieter Hallervorden — an actor and comedian who is a household name in Germany, and who was born in Dessau in Saxony-Anhalt nearly 91 years ago.

Hallervorden, not previously known as a CDU supporter, has now joined Schulze on stage during the election campaign four times. The venues were packed, and the events easily ranked among the best-attended of Schulze's campaign. The comedian showed no compunctions about criticizing the federal government's defense and arms export policies. During one of his musical performances, an image of protesters bearing a banner with the slogan "Stop the genocide in Gaza" was briefly visible in the background.

Schulze calmly rejected sharp criticism of this from his party's headquarters in Berlin. He maintained that he did not share, and even rejected some of Hallervorden's views, but had shared the stage with him to demonstrate his commitment to freedom of speech. The AfD, Schulze noted, seeks to abolish freedom of speech, while he does not.

The threat to German culture

Dessau is known around the world as being one of the homes of the Bauhaus movement, which propelled art and architecture into the modern era starting in 1919. The Nazis sought to stifle the movement when they took power in 1933.

Now, 90 years later, some members of the AfD have again been directly echoing the Nazis' language about the famous movement: In a speech to the state parliament last year, AfD representative Hans Thomas Tillschneider described Bauhaus as a "wrong track of modernism" — a direct quote from the 1928 book Art and Race by architecture critic Paul Schultze-Naumburg, who influenced Nazi thought.

Schulze has accused the AfD of wanting to return to Germany's past eras of oppression, and sought to tie the far-right party to East Germany's communist dictatorship. "When the AfD sings the GDR anthem at the end of its party events, it shows exactly what it wants: a return to the days of the GDR," Schulze told DW. "And I do not want us to wall ourselves in again, as happened here before. That is not what the people want."

Running a local campaign

At campaign events, Schulze attempts to shift the focus away from federal or global political issues and toward the situation within the state of Saxony-Anhalt. He often cites local businesses that rely on foreign employees and on exports to worldwide markets. Regarding healthcare and care for the elderly, he warns against simply adopting, without debate, the recommendations of a commission appointed by the federal government. That again directly contravened Merz's message, who said that those recommendations, which some say contain several cuts to public services, should and would be followed to the letter.

Much Schulze remains undeterred, and has vowed to keep discussing the issues that matter to the people of Saxony-Anhalt. "I trust the people here," he said. He says he is counting on the people of Saxony-Anhalt to stand up against having their state "turned upside down." Sometimes, he says the election boils down to "Sven Schulze or the AfD."

This article has been translated from German.

entries.title: Modi-Putin meeting at SCO: Can India-Russia ties hold?
entries.summary: Indian PM Modi meets Russia's President Putin at the SCO summit in Bishkek as Moscow and New Delhi face rising tensions with Washington — Russia over war-related sanctions, and India over its energy and trade choices.
entries.content:
India

Modi-Putin meeting at SCO: Can India-Russia ties hold?

August 31, 2026

Indian PM Modi and Russian President Putin are at the SCO summit in Bishkek as Moscow and New Delhi face rising tensions with Washington — Russia over war-related sanctions, and India over its energy and trade choices.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Russian President Vladimir Putin are set to meet in Kyrgyzstan's capital Bishkek on Monday on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit — a bloc often seen as a counterweight to US influence.

The meeting comes against the backdrop of the fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted global energy markets, and Russia's war in Ukraine, which is in its fifth year.

India has remained engaged with the SCO while resisting efforts to turn it into an anti-Western bloc. Its position reflects a broader effort to maintain relationships with competing powers.

That approach is under greater pressure. Russiaremains under Western sanctions over the war in Ukraine. Meanwhile, India has faced US pressure over its purchases of Russian oil, alongside wider trade tensions.

A former Indian ambassador to the US, Meera Shankar, told DW that India's relationship with Russia should not be seen as directed against the US.

"India has a long-standing strategic relationship with Russia. This is not directed against any country but intended to help India meet its national goals," said Shankar.

Energy ties deepen

Energy has become the most visible change in the India-Russia relationship. 

Before 2022, when Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it supplied only a small share of India's crude imports. Discounted Russian oil rapidly changed that, making Moscow one of India's biggest suppliers.

It has also become the most contentious part of India's relationship with the US, which has pressed New Delhi to reduce its purchases from Russia India maintains that securing affordable and reliable energy is a national interest.

The disruption to traditional energy supplies has made that calculation more complicated. This year's US-Israel war on Iran and disruption of traffic through the Strait of Hormuz have affected India's purchases from the Gulf and pushed up prices.

Shankar says India is responding by diversifying its sources of supply, including Russia and the US.

"In the long run, a transition to a non-fossil fuel economy would strengthen India's energy independence. But this will not happen overnight," she added.

Until then, Shankar said, India will take steps it considers necessary to stabilize supplies and protect its people.

The future of India-Russia defense cooperation

Defense remains the other major pillar, but here the direction of travel is clearer: India's dependence on Russian equipment has been declining.

The Ukraine war has raised questions over Russia's production capacity, delivery schedules and ability to supply spare parts after decades as a major supplier of India's military hardware.

"India remains one of Russia's oldest and largest arms buyers, and perhaps the last major one," Aravind Yelery, an associate professor at Jawaharlal Nehru University in the Indian capital New Delhi, told DW.

"New Delhi is increasingly reluctant to commit to Russia's fifth-generation fighter program and has little appetite for new Russian hardware unless it can be incorporated into India's indigenous production plans," he added.

While India has diversified its purchases, that does not mean the defense relationship is disappearing.

However, the terms are changing, with India looking for a relationship that contributes to its own defense production, so that it can move away from simply buying finished systems.

The China question

Russia's growing dependence on China has also become an unavoidable part of the India-Russia equation.

Since the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, China has become indispensable to Russia as a market, supplier and economic partner. That has reduced Moscow's ability to serve as a counterweight to Beijing.

Yelery sees an important distinction in the two relationships.

"Strategically, Russia's relationship with China remains structurally transactional, a dependence it can ill afford to compromise, whereas its relationship with India rests on partnership," he said.

India still has reasons to keep Moscow close: energy, defense, access to the Russian market and a longstanding political relationship across Eurasia. But the strategic calculation has changed.

India's 'America plus' strategy

Strategic affairs expert C Raja Mohan saysthat Russia's growing dependence on China has changed its strategic value for India.

"Russia is no longer in a position to help India balance China," the professor of American Studies at Jindal Global University told DW.

This changes India's expectations from the relationship with Russia.

The emphasis is increasingly on specific interests — energy security, defense supplies, trade, and access to technology — while India's larger strategic weight increasingly rests on relationships with the US and its allies.

India has expanded defense and technology cooperation with Washington, while deepening ties with partners such as France and Israel.

Mohan describes this approach as an "America plus" strategy, whereby India maintains its partnership with the US while widening its engagement with other major powers.

"India is trying to reduce its exposure to American volatility, but it still recognizes that Washington is its most important partner," he said.

What do Modi and Putin want?

Rajan Kumar, a professor of Russian studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University, said that Putin wants reassurance that India will remain engaged with Moscow despite pressure from Washington.

"President Putin needs an assurance from Prime Minister Modi that India will not ditch Russia when the latter is facing the worst possible crisis after the 1990s," Kumar told DW.

He expects continuity rather than a dramatic reset. "I think it is more about continuation of existing ties amid US pressure," Kumar added.

Energy trade and payment mechanisms, ways to increase Indian exports to Russia, defense cooperation and the two countries' assessments of the conflicts in Ukraine and Iran are likely to remain important.

The bigger test will come in Delhi in September, when Putin is expected to return for the BRICS summit.

The Bishkek meeting can keep the political relationship on track, but the Delhi talks will show whether that political continuity can produce progress on trade, energy, defense and technology.

The relationship is no longer what it was before the Ukraine war. Energy has become far more important, India's defense dependence is being recalibrated, and Russia's closeness to China has altered the strategic equation.

"The relationship has a value that goes beyond individual deals. Putin appears well aware that India carries an independent strategic weight that China's structural leverage cannot substitute," said Yelery.

Edited by: Emmy Sasipornkarn

entries.title: Italy extends Schengen suspension with Spain
entries.summary: Italy's far-right government announced that it will continue to exclude Spanish nationals from the free movement agreement for another 15 days.
entries.content:
Spain

Italy extends Schengen suspension with Spain

August 31, 2026

Italy's far-right government announced that it will continue to exclude Spanish nationals from the free movement agreement for another 15 days.

The government of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni will extend its suspension of the Schengen free movement agreement with Spain for another 15 days at least, Italian media reported on Monday.

Rome had already suspended the arrangement with Madrid for a month beginning on July 31, in response to an influx of migrants who crossed into the Spanish territory of Ceuta.

The incident, in which dozens of migrants died, triggered a massive European Union migration emergency and brought Spain's leftist government much criticism, including from Italy.

What else do we know about Italy's extension?

Italy's Interior Ministry said the decision to extend the suspension was taken "due to the persistence of the factors that had led to the reintroduction of the measures on Aug. 1," without clarifying.

The ministry added that Italy was aware of "the steps already undertaken ⁠by ​Spain, together with the European Union, to ​help bring the situation in the area back to normal in the ​near future."

The announcement came despite the fact that nearly all of the some 70,000 people who had broken through the barrier returned to Morocco in the days after the incident. 

Spain had responded to Italy's suspension by introducing its own border controls for passengers arriving from Italy and on Monday reportedly said it was extending this measure by 15 days, in an apparent tit-for-tat move.

Sanchez says Ceuta incident traced to Russian, Israeli agents

Socialist Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said on Monday that an "international far-right movement" with "links to Russia and Israel" had created a disinformation campaign on social media that led to the incident at the border fence in Ceuta.

Both Rabat and Madrid had earlier said that the crisis was exacerbated by incorrect information circulating on social media regarding a recent Supreme Court ruling.

"What we know so far is that a ruling by the Supreme Court of July 8 was distorted, which was spread on social networks through fake news, disinformation and also by criminal organizations that traffic in people," Sanchez told broadcaster SER on Monday.

He said there had been a concerted effort "to attack and divide not only Spain but also Europe," without providing further details.

Sanchez added that there was no evidence that Moroccan authorities had been responsible.

Some 5,000 migrants remain in Ceuta, Sanchez said, with at least 1,200 being minors.

On Friday, Spain asked for help from the European Border and Coast Guard Agency (Frontex) in processing the remaining migrants, amid rising protests against their presence by residents of the exclave.

Ceuta is bordered by Morocco on one side and the sea on the other, with no direct access to the mainland of the European Union, making it difficult for any asylum seekers to access the bloc from there.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: Nepal floods: A major test for PM Balen's government
entries.summary: A year after Gen Z-led protests swept Prime Minister Balendra "Balen" Shah to power, deadly floods are testing his government's ability to manage a national crisis.
entries.content:
Nepal

Nepal floods test PM Balen's young government

August 31, 2026

A year after Gen Z-led protests swept Prime Minister Balendra "Balen" Shah to power, deadly floods are testing his government's ability to manage a national crisis.

Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah, an ex-rapper popularly known as "Balen," is facing the enormous task of rebuilding communities and critical infrastructure following last week's deadly flash floods.

The floods, carrying rock, ice, mud and debris, swept through areas near the Chinese border, ravaging entire towns and damaging hydropower plants.

More than 900 people have been killed and nearly 4,800 remain missing, authorities said Monday, as rescue efforts entered a sixth day.

The devastating floods struck the Himalayan nation just days before the anniversary of the Gen-Z-led anti-corruption protests of September 8-9 last year that toppled the previous government and swept Shah to power.

Now, the 36-year-old prime minister and his largely inexperienced cabinet face their first major national crisis in what is shaping up to be the country's worst disaster in a decade.

Anxious relatives await news from flood zone

Rescuers, including Chinese and Indian experts, believe hundreds of workers are trapped in tunnels at hydropower sites under construction that were buried in mud by the catastrophic flooding. 

Sushila Giri was waiting for news of her son, Sishir, a Kathmandu University student completing an internship at one of the hydropower projects.

"I came to know that my son, along with others, was at the quarter of the hydro project when the disaster happened," she told DW. "Please help me find his whereabouts."

Gen Z activist Raksha Bam expressed concern about delays in rescuing workers trapped at hydropower projects and urged the government to seek specialized assistance from the international community.

Across affected districts, family members gathered in hospitals and temporary aid centers hoping for news of missing loved ones.

Indra Adhikari lost her home and paddy fields in the floods. Four of her relatives remain missing. She said rescue and relief efforts appeared concentrated in areas accessible by road and where media were present, particularly along one side of the Trishuli River.

"Most of those who have come to Trishuli Bazar are not rescuers but onlookers," she told DW. "Remote settlements farther upstream and across the river remain difficult to reach."

How is the new government handling the crisis?

The administration itself has acknowledged that it was not fully prepared for a disaster of such scale, which is the deadliest for Nepal since a 2015 earthquake killed thousands and injured many more.

"On the very first day, we got a bit confused as to how to deal with the crisis," Minister for Information and Communication Bikram Timilsina told DW after visiting the flood-hit area. "[From the] second day onwards, we have been putting all our efforts into swift search, rescue and relief works."

Security agencies have received praise for their response, particularly their efforts to reach people in inaccessible areas via helicopters. But the disaster has also exposed questions about the government's crisis-management capacity and its relationship with Nepal's provincial and local governments.

"Given the scale of devastation, the government's efforts and promptness to deal with the crisis are commendable," Madhu Raman Acharya, a former foreign secretary of Nepal, told DW. "The preliminary search and rescue efforts, especially coordination among security agencies, are commendable."

Govinda Pokharel, a former chief executive officer of the National Reconstruction Authority, which oversaw post-earthquake reconstruction, however, has a different take.

He said that the federal government had attempted to manage the crisis largely on its own, without adequately involving local and provincial governments. This is particularly significant because Shah's ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party has no presence in local or provincial governments.

Pokharel also questioned whether the government's lack of experience had affected its ability to gauge the scale of the response required.

"Our neighboring countries like China and India were willing to lend help for rescue, especially for tunnel-rescue from the very outset," he told DW, adding that the government failed to decide in time whether to allow them to deploy, costing three crucial days.

Can Balen's government deliver?

Nepal initially maintained that its own rescue teams were capable of handling the operation.

But by Friday, Foreign Minister Shishir Khanal told the media that the government had decided to seek international expertise, including from China and India, for tunnel rescues, DNA testing and forensic examinations.

The shift highlighted one of the central challenges facing the new administration: whether the government can act quickly and effectively during a rapidly evolving national emergency.

Pokharel said the government's decision to raise substantial funds domestically for disaster relief demonstrated public confidence.

"One good thing is that the government is collecting a huge sum of public money domestically on the Prime Minister's Disaster Relief Fund," he said. "It shows the public trust in the government that doesn't misuse its funds collected in the name of relief."

By Saturday, over 5 billion Nepali rupees ($34.7 million, €29.9 million) had been collected in a government-run disaster relief fund for flood victims, according to the Office of the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers.

Prabha Bogati, deputy mayor of Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot, said local authorities had limited scope to act during the crisis because the federal government adopted a centralized "one-door" approach, requiring relief activities to be coordinated through a single command structure.

"In previous crises, local communities and volunteers used to be mobilized in search, rescue and relief efforts," she told DW.

Bogati added that helicopter rescues have been effective, but local stakeholders have not been brought into the response and have not been allowed to recover bodies or perform final rites.

Government spokesperson and Education Minister Sasmit Pokharel defended the administration's response, saying all available resources were being mobilized for rescue, relief and rehabilitation.

"In the first phase, our priority was to save citizens' lives by using the available human resources and means," Pokharel told reporters. "A process has also been initiated to better organize the mobilization of volunteers."

Edited by: Keith Walker

entries.title: Niger: Failed coup exposes junta's weakness — and Russia's influence
entries.summary: The failed coup in Niger brings deep divisions within the military to light. As Russia's support highlights the junta's fading influence, soldiers continue to face jihadist attacks, poor equipment and little pay.
entries.content:
Niger

Niger's failed coup exposes cracks in the military

August 31, 2026

The failed coup in Niger brings deep divisions within the military to light. As Russia's support highlights the junta's fading influence, soldiers continue to face jihadist attacks, poor equipment and little pay.

What does it mean to be a soldier in Niger today? It means fighting jihadist groups under difficult conditions and at considerable personal risk.

At the same time, military personnel are expected to follow a strict military leadership which only came to power through a coup.

At the top of this junta sits General Abdourahamane Tiani, the erstwhile commander of the presidential guard prior to the military takeover in 2023.

Tiani ousted democratically elected President Mohamed Bazoum, with his junta largely justifying its rule by invoking the ongoing fight against jihadist violence in the country, which it claims the Bazoum administration had failed to sufficiently address.

But the failed uprising in Niamey puts that claim to the test amid growing frustration within the military over the unending battle against Islamist insurgencies.

On the weekend, parts of the army temporarily took control of Air Base 101 at Niamey's international airport, and attempted to advance toward the Presidential Palace and Niger's state broadcaster.

The government has described the incident as a mutiny.

But Senegalese governance expert Pape Ibrahima Kane told DW in an exclusive interview that "this was not just a mutiny, but an attempted coup. If this is not an attempted coup, then what does an attempted coup look like?"

Growing frustration within the army

Niger's military has been fighting jihadist groups for years without managing to contain the violence.

The capital Niamey itself has come under attack several times this year alone.

For soldiers, this means that they're exposed to high risks daily, compounded by serious problems with equipment, supplies and logistics.

Kane describes an army struggling to move its troops and equipment across the country's vast territory. Whether the government has the financial resources to address these shortcomings meanwhile remains an open question.

There also appears to be growing frustration over military pay and work conditions.

Sahel expert Mamadou Mouth Bane sees the possible preferential treatment of the presidential guard over frontline units as one factor behind the discontent that resulted in the uprising.

"The men who are at the front are being neglected. They feel forgotten and treated worse" than the presidential units, Bane explained in a DW interview, highlighting that the junta cannot afford to alienate these soldiers.

The military uprising also highlights the junta's chief dilemma: The loyalty of its forces remain key to the current military rulers' ongoing grip on power, which in the light of the latest developments might just be slipping.

Russia: Niger's security guarantor

The role of Russia's Africa Corps is also particularly significant in this context.

The force has taken over large parts of the former activities of Wagnar mercenaries in Africa.

Following the failed mutiny against the Kremlin of Wagner Group chief Yevgeny Prigozhin and mysterious his death in a plane crash in August 2023, Russia quickly reorganized its operations in Africa, placing them more firmly under the control of its defense ministry.

In Niger, the Africa Corps has become an important security partner of the junta. During the latest uprising, Russian forces actively helped retake Air Base 101, according to a statement Russia's ambassador — at the direct behest of the country's military rulers.

By helping the Nigerien army put down an attack from within its own ranks, it is becoming evident that the role of the Africa Corps now reaches well beyond their stated objective of assisting with the military government's counterterrorism strategy.

Kane described Niger's reliance on the Africa Corps as a "strategic dependency" in his exclusive interview with DW, claiming that the junta would have fallen without Russian assistance.

"Without the Russian army, we would have a new government in Niger today," he stressed.

Is Tiani playing Russian roulette?

But there are further factors to take into consideration, which could challenge Kane's statement.

According to DW information gathered on the ground, the presidential guard and other forces loyal to the regime were also heavily involved in the response to the coup attempt.

Algeria — Niger's neighbor to the northwest — meanwhile also backed Niamey, deploying four Su-30 fighter jets to Niger.

The involvement of the Africa Corps was probably a decisive factor in the rapid suppression of the uprising, but not the only one, although it appears to have exposed Tiani's dependence on a foreign armed partner to ensure his grip on power.

A risk for the Sahel at large

It is evident that the Africa Corps alone cannot defeat the ongoing insurgency of jihadist groups; otherwise it would have solved the crisis by now after years of involvement in the region. Neither can it solve the Nigerien army's structural problems.

This makes Niger a test case for the strength of this security model pursued by the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), which is comprised of Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso.

All three military juntas have increasingly been turning to Russia while distancing themselves from Western partners.

But Russian support can only help stabilize the juntas in the short term. As long as foreign forces have to take over critical security tasks, the underlying causes of the military crisis remain unresolved.

The failed coup attempt was ultimately a victory for Tiani's junta — but equally a warning sign about the state of Niger's armed forces, as in the face of mounting challenges, their loyalty to the regime can clearly no longer be taken for granted.

Edited by: Sertan Sanderson

entries.title: Swiss police arrest man over deadly rave shooting
entries.summary: One woman was killed and several others were injured in a shooting at a rave in the Swiss town of Aarau over the weekend. Police say a 43-year-old suspect has been arrested.
entries.content:
August 31, 2026

One woman was killed and several others were injured in a shooting at a rave in the Swiss town of Aarau over the weekend. Police say a 43-year-old suspect has been arrested.

Swiss police on Monday arrested a suspect in the weekend shooting at a rave in the Swiss town of Aarau, where an Italian woman was killed and several others were injured.

Local police had said the incident could have been an act of terrorism, but that other motives were also being considered. The attack came after the party had officially ended, but at least 100 people were still at the event location when the shooting began.

Authorities said that the suspect was a Swiss national, and that they believe he acted alone.

What do we know about the arrest made?

"Investigations ‌into the exact ‌circumstances ​of the incident, as well as its ​background and possible motive, are currently ⁠underway. ​At this ​stage, it is ​assumed that ‌a single perpetrator was involved," ​police ⁠in the canton ⁠of ​Aargau said in a statement.

Police added that the suspect was arrested on "strong suspicion" of being behind the attack.

At least five others were injured in the attack, some seriously.

Investigators found two kinds of cartridges at the scene, indicating the presence of a pistol and a large weapon, possibly an assault rifle.

The suspect was apprehended after a major manhunt, which also involved police from neighboring Germany.

Edited by: Rana Taha

entries.title: With multilateralism in decline, what's next for the world?
entries.summary: The global political architecture is shifting, partly as a result of the actions of US President Donald Trump. As nations search for a new world order, some may gain influence and power, while others have much to lose.
entries.content:
United States of America

With multilateralism in decline, what's next for the world?

August 31, 2026

The global political architecture is shifting, partly as a result of the actions of US President Donald Trump. As nations search for a new world order, some may gain influence and power, while others have much to lose.

Donald Trump's visit to UN headquarters in New York in September 2025 was rife with symbolism.

As the US president stepped onto the escalator in the lobby ahead of his address, it stopped working. Then, the teleprompter failed during his speech, prompting the former TV star to tell the assembled heads of state and government, half-jokingly: "These are the two things I got from the United Nations: A bad escalator and a bad teleprompter."

The United Nations is the central institution of the post-World War II order, shaped in part by the United States and based on multilateralism and the balancing of interests. When the UN was founded in 1945, its goal was to prevent wars. Its mandate later expanded to include countless other areas, such as global health, development and climate protection.

Today, more than 80 years later, the UN's institutions, above all the Security Council, are widely considered to be in need of an overhaul, much like the UN headquarters itself.

The broken escalator incident was apparently triggered accidentally by Trump's own camera operator, the UN has said, rejecting responsibility for the incident. And beyond this symbolic moment, views are split over whether Trump, with his sometimes isolationist America First ideology, is above all a symptom of the crumbling multilateral world order or a destructive wrecking ball.

Far beyond escalators and teleprompters, politicians and analysts around the world are debating the question: Is multilateralism coming to an end — and if so, what comes next?

A new world order in five years or continued disorder?

Finnish President Alexander Stubb, one of the few heads of state to hold a doctorate in international relations, argues that the world is currently experiencing a power vacuum from which a new world order will likely emerge over the next five years.

Other experts expect a longer period of adjustment. "It is time to acknowledge that the old order really has disappeared and to plot a new approach to geopolitics. This moment does not constitute a short interregnum between a US-led order and a Chinese-led one," Mark Leonard, director of the European Council on Foreign Relations think tank, recently wrote in an essay in Foreign Affairs magazine.

"For some time, the world will be without any order at all, swept by fragmentation, contagion, and strangulation or the temptation to weaponize a wide variety of geographic, economic, and technological chokepoints."

An era of reform gridlock

"That framework of multilateralism, which is connected with the world after World War II [...] and a golden period of then the United Nations, I would say that it's all over," said Teresa Nogueira Pinto, a globalization expert specializing in Africa at Lusofona University in Lisbon.

"It's not working," she added. "We can see that in the peacekeeping and peacebuilding missions, most of them, they have been a failure, and then we see that the UN is desperately in need of a reform."

Speaking with DW, Pinto cited the UN Security Council as an example, stressing that it doesn't represent the world in 2026. "But who would join? India, Pakistan, Nigeria, Ethiopia — I mean, it's very, very hard to even imagine a reform."

Johannes Thimm, head of the Americas Research Group at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin, takes a different view. "I do not agree that this era is already completely over," he said. "International law is very diverse and also includes a great deal that you don't even notice in the daily relations between states, diplomatic conventions, treaties and so on. And there is still quite a lot there that you don't really notice because it isn't particularly spectacular."

But he added that there is no doubt that international law has increasingly been violated in recent times, for example, through wars of aggression in Ukraine and Iran. Meanwhile, violations of international humanitarian law, as in Gaza, also pose a challenge to the multilateral order.

Thimm pointed out US withdrawals from dozens of international organizations and treaties as another factor undermining the stability of multilateralism. These include the World Health Organization, the Paris climate agreement, the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change and the UN Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO). Just recently, the US government further stepped up its pressure on the International Criminal Court, which it has criticized.

"If the still most powerful state acts this way," Thimm said, "then that poses a threat to the system as a whole. So, I would say, a greater threat than when Russia, for example, wages a war of aggression."

Old alliances fray, new ones emerge

Trump frequently invokes the Monroe Doctrine of 1823, which defined the Western Hemisphere as an exclusive sphere of influence for Washington. Applied to the present day, this could mean that the rest of the world is no longer dominated by the United States but by other major and middle powers: that's to say a multipolar world order following the departure of the US as the dominant power.

For many countries, this upheaval carries the risk of losing influence. For others, however, it can also be an incentive to reposition themselves and secure their place through alliances of their own in a multipolar world no longer dominated by the West. It is no coincidence, for example, that the BRICS alliance of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa has also gained in importance and taken on new members. It is increasingly seeking to establish a confident counterweight to the Western-dominated international financial architecture.

"Many African countries are realizing that the previous models were not so advantageous for them, and especially for growth and sustainable growth," said Pinto. "They are taking advantage of this, and I would say also that this is very connected to the comeback of geopolitics. For a period we thought that geopolitics was history, but it's not."

The world is also reorganizing itself in terms of security policy. Within NATO, there are fears of a further US withdrawal or even a military attack from within should Trump continue to pursue hi sclaims to Greenland, which is administered by Denmark. In the Indo-Pacific region, and especially in the Middle East, US allies are questioning the reliability of American security guarantees and looking for new alliances.

In early August, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and nuclear-armed Pakistan launched the Mecca Defense Pact, with NATO-style mutual defense guarantees. The agreement, as well as the European coalition of the willing to support Ukraine, are seen as examples of the smaller, more agile formats that are sometimes referred to as "minilateralism."

In many cases, military and diplomatic efforts are being considered together. "A world without rules only helps the strong," said SWP expert Thimm. "Everyone else, whether they are moderately strong or weak, gets crushed. And that is why Europe, which I would count among the moderately strong, naturally has a strong interest in preserving some kind of order."

Alongside military considerations, many states are also looking for new, broader economic and political partnerships. Pinto expects regional alliances to gain importance and potentially produce better results than mechanisms at the global level. The World Trade Organization, for example, achieved a great deal in the 20th century, she said, but has not functioned for some time now.

"Now, it may be more useful to think about regional approaches such as the African Continental Free Trade Area."

The harmonization of African markets is seen as a promising approach to solving many problems. But further implementation of the free trade area, ratified by almost all African states since 2018, has been rather slow.

Whose interests will a future world order serve?

Pinto said three factors could influence the future distribution of power in a multipolar world: sovereignty, access to resources and, last but not least, demographics. Young, growing societies in Africa and Asia could make themselves indispensable. "India could become a superpower by the end of the century," she said.

Amid the decline of US influence, the growing power of other actors such as China, and other factors including minilateralism and regional alliances — it's still too early to say for sure what kind of world order will emerge from the status quo.

At least in the short term, however, Thimm fears that "the world will become more violent. There will be more wars. The wars will become more brutal. It will be more difficult to organize cooperation. So I don't know what will happen when the next pandemic breaks out. I don't know what will happen when the next global financial crisis breaks out."

Against this backdrop, he pointed out that we still face the climate crisis, a key challenge that can only be solved through collective action.

This article was originally published in German.

entries.title: Inside the sea cucumber smuggling boom
entries.summary: A quiet multimillion‑dollar black market is exploding across the Indian Ocean, driven by one unlikely animal: the sea cucumber.
entries.content:
August 31, 2026

A quiet multimillion‑dollar black market is exploding across the Indian Ocean, driven by one unlikely animal: the sea cucumber.

When it comes to smuggling, squishy sea blobs that spend their lives eating and pooping are probably not what comes to mind. But a group of lumpen creatures known as sea cucumbers are at the center of a $200 million (€175 million) black market trade.

Known alternately and misleadingly as sea cucumbers or sand fish, they are actually neither cucumbers nor fish, but echinoderms. In other words, invertebrate marine animals with a skin or a hard covering.

Found in abundance around the Andaman Islands — the easternmost landmass of the Indian territory —  local biologist Sangamesh Uday says they are so ecologically important that without them the intertidal zone "wouldn't be an ecosystem, it would just be broken rocks."

The 1,500 or so species of sea cucumber around the world are great marine recyclers. They eat organic material including bacteria and microalgae, break it down, and excrete clean oxygenated sand. This keeps vital nutrients like nitrogen and phosphorous in circulation and suppresses coral diseases.

It also boosts ocean alkalinity levels which helps to slow down acidification, which is becoming a huge issue as rising levels of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere cause oceans to warm. In short, it's hard to overstate the environmental importance of these innocuous looking lumps.

Why are they being smuggled?

To their detriment, sea cucumbers are also considered a delicacy, especially in China and Southeast Asia. Historical records show they were traded between Indonesian fishers and Chinese merchants even 800 years ago.



They are used in soups, served as pickled sides or turned into traditional medicine.  And though there is some scientific evidence that the Omega-3 they contain is a useful antioxidant and anti-inflammatory, they're mostly popular because they're quite phallic — and therefore considered an aphrodisiac.

Since the 1980s, commercial sea cucumber harvesting has expanded globally, with better access as well as higher incomes and demand in East Asia acting as the main drivers. Though many countries have outlawed the practice, some like Sri Lanka and Madagascar do allow fishing and aquaculture. Of the existing sea cucumber fisheries, 70% have become overexploited globally.

The combination of the increasing demand and legal complexities has drawn the attention of minor and major mafias. Some of the largest Mexican cartels and even the Japanese Yakuza have been reported as diversifying their portfolios by using sea cucumbers and other sea creatures to keep the money flowing.

These illicit groups enter every aspect of the supply chain — from extorting fishermen to the final smuggling of illegally-caught cucumbers across borders.

They exploit weak environmental regulations and a lack of official knowledge around rules and species. Sea cucumbers are sometimes marked as legal fish consignments or smuggled into countries that do allow trade in the species.

Leading expert on sea cucumber crime, Teale Phelps Bondaroff, says awareness is critical in dealing with the issue.

"While many law enforcement officers may be on the lookout for drugs, weapons, or well-known wildlife contraband like ivory, rhino horns, or shark fins, sea cucumbers may slip past," he tells DW.

Poachers from overseas drawn to the Andaman Islands

The Indian government began regulating sea cucumbers in the 1980s and introduced a blanket ban on fishing them in 2001, when it saw the impact of the illicit trade on local populations.

Since then, India has become the country with the strongest protections for the species. Anyone who catches one faces a seven-year jail term — the same sentence handed down for poaching a tiger or elephant.

As a result, sea cucumbers close to the Andaman Islands have generally thrived. In the ocean around Myanmar, around 50km (30 miles) further north, it's a different picture. Civil war in the country has severely impacted local livelihoods and local black-market agents are using the instability to offer comparatively higher sums for a boatload of illegally caught sea cucumbers. And as their numbers in local waters dwindle, poachers head south.



It is no easy game, however. They have to dodge the Indian coast guard, navy, police, evade local fishermen and even dense populations of crocodiles.

They survive on fish, freediving using hookah pipes to breathe, and spend months rationing their diesel to ensure they have enough to make it back home — evading the Myanmar authorities and pirates looking to try and steal their catch.

Many poachers are caught by the regional Andaman and Nicobar police, who are being specifically trained to comb the mangrove islands to find them. At least 50 people have been arrested in the past year, some as young as 16 and some in their 60s. Several have come back for the second or third time — risking being incarcerated again after completing full sentences.

Is there a way to stop the illegal trade?

Despite the efforts of the Indian authorities, the number of poachers coming in, year after year, has stayed stable.

Bondaroff sees a need to sound the alarm at a global level. Other similar trades, like that of shark fins, have been slowed thanks to increased awareness about its cruelty and impact on the ecosystem — making it less socially acceptable.  



"The solution must include educating consumers about the harms of unsustainable and illegal sea cucumber extraction and tackling seafood fraud."

Other suggestions include India opening up small areas of its waters where sea cucumbers can be legally fished, or introducing community-based aquaculture that is easier to regulate and would also benefit local fishers.

But Bondaroff thinks that tackling the problem also requires cooperation and a deep understanding of the issue.



"This means liaising and information sharing between governments and law enforcement agencies," he says. "And working together to address the complex financial crimes that enable sea cucumber crime." 

This report was supported by the Pulitzer Center.



Edited by: Tamsin Walker

entries.title: Ailing Djokovic 'despised' every moment of US Open defeat
entries.summary: Novak Djokovic has exited in the first round of a Grand Slam for the first time in over two decades. Could time — or an unknown health condition — be catching up with the Serbian tennis legend?
entries.content:
August 31, 2026

Novak Djokovic has exited in the first round of a Grand Slam for the first time in over two decades. Could time — or an unknown health condition — be catching up with the Serbian tennis legend?

Former world No.1 Novak Djokovic's US Open has ended with this earliest Grand Slam exit in two decades as he fell to Mariano Navone 7-6 (7/5), 5-7, 4-6, 6-2, 6-1 on Sunday.

The defeat scuppered the Serbian tennis legend's latest bid for a 25th Grand Slam title, and ended a streak of 78 Grand Slam first-round victories, which began at the 2006 French Open.

Considering the obvious discomfort the 39-year-old Djokovic began feeling early in the match, it was truly impressive that he managed to take Navone, 25, the distance.

After battling through more than four and a half hours in the Arthur Ashe Stadium, Djokovic gracefully congratulated his opponent.

"I don't want to take too much out of his win. Congrats to him. He's a nice guy, a fighter," Djokovic said of the 25-year-old Argentine, currently 48th in the men's rankings.

"It's unbelievable," Navone said after triumphing in his first meeting with his childhood idol.

 "It was a tough match, a battle. Playing against Novak the first time in the biggest stage we have in the world of tennis right now… I mean, it's crazy."

I 'despised' every minute

Throughout most of the match, Djokovic looked physically spent, repeatedly throwing up into a courtside bucket and regularly doubling over in pain.

Unsurprisingly, Djokovic said he had "despised" every moment of the ordeal at Flushing Meadows.

"I think it was obvious that it was an awful feeling on the court for me," he said.

"It's something that I've been carrying, unfortunately, pretty much every match this year. You know, vomiting, throwing up, a serious issue there.

"Then my whole body, you know, starts to collapse, basically cramping and pain. Yeah, the back just gave up in the end and shoulder, and I couldn't close it out?"

Long-term 'health issue'

His last tournament, in Cincinnati two weeks ago, where Djokovic threw up into a towel, first revealed that he had been struggling with a "health issue" that affects him in hot, humid conditions for "many years."

Despite the unspecified medical condition he suffers from, Djokovic reached the final of the Australian Open in January and the semifinals of Wimbledon in June. However, he said following his exit in New York that he's now simply not physically capable of going deep into tournaments.

This mystery ailment, coupled with his age, will have many asking whether Djokovic, who remarkably still sits at No. 5 in the men's rankings, could be approaching the end.

Perhaps more alarming than the ailment itself is the fact that he simply doesn't know how to correct the problem. Still, he appears determined to battle on — at least for now.

"Can the issue be fixed? I don't know," he said.

"I'm trying, man. I'm trying. Let's see."
